--- title: "Data Visualization" subtitle: "POL 051 F26 A04, A05, & A06 2026" author: "Haley Daarstad" footer: "[haleydaarstad.com/pol051-su26/](http://haleydaarstad.com/pol051-su26/)" logo: "images/logo.png" format: revealjs: slide-number: true height: 900 width: 1600 code-line-numbers: true smooth-scrawl: true theme: [simple, html/custom.scss] incremental: true title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: img/dubois-spiral-2.png data-background-size: contain data-background-position: right data-background-color: "#dc354a" --- ## Why visualize data? ::: incremental - Data carries **weight** in our society - **Visualizing** data is an effective way to convey information, convince, argue - Visualization can be used to tell **The Truth™️** (or not) ::: # Making graphs in `R` {background-color="#dc354a"} ## The **grammar** of graphics {.center} . . . Graphs have an internal logic, or **grammar** that connects data to visuals . . . **Data** = variables in a dataset . . . **Aesthetic** = visual property of a graph (position, shape, color, etc.) . . . **Geometry** = representation of an aesthetic (point, line, text, etc.) ## Mapping data to aesthetics ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Data |Aesthetic |Geometry | |:---------------|:-----------------|:--------| |GDP per capita |Position(x-axis) |Point | |Life expectancy |Position (y-axis) |Point | |Continent |Color |Point | |Population |Size |Point | ::: ::: 1. Take the **data**, 2. map it onto an **aesthetic**, 3. and visualize it with a **geometry** ## In R ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Data |aes() |geom_ | |:---------|:-----|:------------| |gdpPercap |x |geom_point() | |lifeExp |y |geom_point() | |continent |color |geom_point() | |pop |size |geom_point() | ::: ::: Use the variable names *exactly* as they appear in the data, map them onto the *exact* function names in R ## `ggplot()`: our first function 😢 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1"} ggplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: don't fret; You will not memorize these as they appear on screen ## `ggplot`: specify the data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = gap_07) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Use `aes()` to map variables to aesthetics ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = gap_07, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## add geometries and layers using `+` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = gap_07, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## mapping population to size in `aes()` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = gap_07, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## mapping continent to color in `aes()` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = gap_07, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## Other layers: add the missing titles with `labs()` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = gap_07, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "GDP per capita", y = "Life expectancy", title = "Global wealth and health in 2007", size = "Population", color = "") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: Notice that text is placed within **quotation marks**! ## Other layers: add a theme ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = gap_07, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "GDP per capita", y = "Life expectancy", title = "Global wealth and health in 2007") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: There are many more themes, [here are a few](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggtheme.html) ## The final formula ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = gap_07, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "GDP per capita", y = "Life expectancy", title = "Global wealth and health in 2007") + theme_bw() ``` ::: 1. Tell `ggplot()` the data we want to plot 2. Map all variables onto aesthetics within `aes()` 3. Add layers like `geom_point()` and `theme_bw()` using `+` # Key plotting questions {.center} - What am I trying to **show**? - (a distribution, a relationship, a comparison, an amount) - What **kind** of variables do I have? - (continuous, discrete, something in between) - What **aesthetics** and **geometries** do I need for this plot? - (x-axis, y-axis, color, size, shape, etc.) ## What kind of variable do I have? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
General Social Survey
id age degree race num_kids
1 47 Bachelor White 3
2 61 High School White 0
3 72 Bachelor White 2
4 43 High School White 4
5 55 Graduate White 2
````` ::: ::: ::: incremental - **Continuous** variables take on lots of values (GDP, population, income, age, etc.) ::: ## What kind of variable do I have? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
General Social Survey
id age degree race num_kids
1 47 Bachelor White 3
2 61 High School White 0
3 72 Bachelor White 2
4 43 High School White 4
5 55 Graduate White 2
````` ::: ::: ::: incremental - *Discrete* or **categorical** variables takes on a few values, often "qualitative" (yes/no, 1/0, race, etc.) ::: ## Graph 1 - The Scatterplot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: . . . The **scatterplot** visualizes the relationship between two **continuous** variables . . . Shows every point in the data, reveals trends and *outliers* ## The grammar of scatterplots ::::::: columns :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: The data | gdpPercap| lifeExp| |---------:|-------:| | 974.58| 43.83| | 5937.03| 76.42| | 6223.37| 72.30| | 4797.23| 42.73| | 12779.38| 75.32| ::: ::: ::: :::: :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Mapping the data |Data |Aesthetic |Geometry | |:---------|:---------|:------------| |gdpPercap |x |geom_point() | |lifeExp |y |geom_point() | ::: ::: ::: :::: :::::::
. . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gap_07, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) + geom_point() ``` ::: Typically, we put the **cause** on the x-axis and the **effect** on the y-axis ## Scatterplots are for *continuous* variables ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: Plot is uninformative because continent is *discrete* (i.e., a category) ## 🇺🇸 The presidents 🇺🇸 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} elections_historic %>% select(year, winner, win_party, ec_pct, popular_pct, two_term) %>% slice_head(n = 4) %>% knitr::kable(caption = "Sample of presidential elections", digits = 2) ``` ::: ## 🇺🇸 🚨 The presidents Your turn 🚨🇺🇸 1. Make a plot of presidential election results using the `elections_historic` dataset 2. \% of popular vote (x-axis, `popular_pct`) and % of electoral college vote (y-axis, `ec_pct`) 3. map the winner's party to the `color` aesthetic, whether or not president served two terms to `shape`, and add labels to each point (use `winner_label`) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("socviz") library(socviz) ?elections_historic ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## 🚨 Your turn: Answer 🚨 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(elections_historic, aes(x = popular_pct, y = ec_pct, color = win_party, shape = two_term, label = winner_label)) + geom_point() + geom_text() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: What's going on here? ## ## Graph 2: the time series ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: The **time series** uses a *line* to show you how a variable (y-axis) moves over time (x-axis) ## The grammar of time series ::::::: columns :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: The data | year| avg_yrs| |----:|-------:| | 1952| 49.06| | 1957| 51.51| | 1962| 53.61| | 1967| 55.68| | 1972| 57.65| ::: ::: ::: :::: :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Mapping the data |Data |Aesthetic |Geometry | |:-------|:---------|:-----------| |year |x |geom_line() | |avg_yrs |y |geom_line() | ::: ::: ::: :::: :::::::
. . . Notice the new geometry, `geom_line()` ## The time series ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(life_yr, aes(x = year, y = avg_yrs)) + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## 🚨 Your turn: 💸Recession💸 🚨 - Look at the `economics` dataset from the `tidyverse` package - Type and run `economics` to see the data - Type and run `?economics` to read about the data - Make a time series of unemployment over time - Can you identify the **recessions**? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## 🚨 Your turn: 💸Recession💸 Answer 🚨 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Multiple time series Sometimes we observe multiple **units** over time; how can we visualize these? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |country |continent | year| lifeExp| pop| gdpPercap| |:-------------|:---------|----:|-------:|---------:|----------:| |United States |Americas | 2002| 77.310| 287675526| 39097.0995| |Ghana |Africa | 1967| 48.072| 8490213| 1125.6972| |Denmark |Europe | 1997| 76.110| 5283663| 29804.3457| |Bolivia |Americas | 2002| 63.883| 8445134| 3413.2627| |Ghana |Africa | 1992| 57.501| 16278738| 925.0602| ::: ::: ## Multiple time series ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = gapminder_sample, aes(x = year, y = lifeExp, color = country)) + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: . . . These are useful for *comparing* **trends** across units (countries, places, people, etc) ## Graph 3: the histogram ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: A **histogram** shows you how a continuous variable is *distributed* ## Interpreting histograms ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-32-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: notes What do we see here? ::: ## The grammar of histograms ::::::: columns :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: The data | lifeExp| |-------:| | 43.83| | 76.42| | 72.30| | 42.73| | 75.32| ::: ::: ::: :::: :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Mapping the data |Data |Aesthetic |Geometry | |:-------|:---------|:----------------| |lifeExp |x |geom_histogram() | ::: ::: ::: :::: :::::::
. . . Notice the new geometry, `geom_histogram()`; and that a histogram *only* uses the x-axis! ## The histogram ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gap_07, aes(x = lifeExp)) + geom_histogram() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-35-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## 🚨 Your turn: organs 🫁🧠 🚨 ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} In some countries, when you die it is **assumed** you want to donate your organs - To not donate, you have to **opt out** - In other countries, when you die it is **assumed** you *do not* want to donate your organs - To not donate, you have to **opt in** ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Sample from organdata
country donors opt
Canada 13.9 In
United States 20.1 In
Netherlands 10.9 In
Australia 12.3 In
Ireland NA In
````` ::: ::: ::: ::::: ## 🚨 Your turn: organs 🫁🧠 🚨 Using the `organdata` dataset: 1. Make a histogram of country's organ donation rate (`donors`) 2. Then set the fill aesthetic to `opt`, whether donors have to opt in or opt out of donating. How does the graph change? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## 🚨 Your turn: organs 🫁🧠 Answer 🚨 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(organdata, aes(x= donors, fill = opt)) + geom_histogram() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-38-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Graph 4: the barplot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-39-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: . . . Barplots place a *category* (place, country, person, etc) on one axis and a *quantity* (amount, average, median, etc.) on another . . . Useful for making **comparisons**, highlighting **differences** ::: notes Why would there be differences across TV consumption? ::: ## The grammar of barplots ::::::: columns :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: The data |marital | tv| |:-------------|----:| |No answer | 2.56| |Never married | 3.11| |Separated | 3.55| |Divorced | 3.09| |Widowed | 3.91| ::: ::: ::: :::: :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Mapping the data |Data |Aesthetic |Geometry | |:-------|:---------|:----------| |tv |x |geom_col() | |marital |y |geom_col() | ::: ::: ::: :::: :::::::
. . . ::: callout-note You could switch the x and y mapping around, but I think categories look better on the y-axis ::: ## The barplot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(tv, aes(y = marital, x = tv)) + geom_col() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-42-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Graph 5: the boxplot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-43-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: . . . Boxplots compare **distributions** of *continuous* variables across groups ::: notes they show us *more* than the barplot which only gives us a quantity for each group ::: ## Compare distributions: the boxplot ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} Boxplots contain a lot of info 🥵: - bold line is the **median** observation - box is the **middle** 50% of observations - thin lines show you min and max value, *except...* - the dots, which are **outlier** observations ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-44-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::::: ::: notes interpret ::: ## The grammar of boxplots ::::::: columns :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: The data |continent | lifeExp| |:---------|-------:| |Asia | 43.83| |Europe | 76.42| |Africa | 72.30| |Africa | 42.73| |Americas | 75.32| ::: ::: ::: :::: :::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Mapping the data |Data |Aesthetic |Geometry | |:--------|:---------|:--------------| |contient |y |geom_boxplot() | |lifeExp |x |geom_boxplot() | ::: ::: ::: :::: :::::::
. . . ::: callout-note You could switch the x and y mapping around, but I think categories look better on the y-axis ::: ## The five(-ish) graphs ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Graph aes() geom_ Purpose
Scatterplot x = cause, y = effect point() Relationships
Time series x = date, y = variable line() Trends
Histogram x = cont. variable histogram() Distributions
Barplot y = category, x = quantity col() Compare amounts
Boxplot y = category, x = cont. variable boxplot() Compare distributions
````` ::: ::: . . . Know how and when to use which! # Making better graphs {background-color="#dc354a"} - We've barely scratched the surface; there's many more aesthetics, geometries, and layers in `ggplot()` - Here are some of my favorite ones - And some ideas for making graphs better ## Showing "movement" using panels ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-48-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: . . . We can use **panels** to show *movement* of a variable across time, space, etc. ::: notes What is this graph showing us? ::: ## Using facet_wrap ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = lifeExp)) + geom_histogram() + facet_wrap(vars(year)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-49-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ::: callout-note Make sure the facetting variable is wrapped in `vars()`! ::: ## Make aesthetics static ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gap_07, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) + geom_point(size = 4, color = "orange", shape = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-50-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: Take your aesthetics out of `aes()` and into `geom()` to make them *static* ## Use different color and fill scales ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = lifeExp, fill = continent)) + geom_histogram() + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-51-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: `scale_fill_brewer()` for `fill`, `scale_color_brewer` for `color` ## My favorite scale (right now) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = lifeExp, fill = continent)) + geom_histogram() + scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "magma") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-52-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: `scale_fill_viridis_d` for *discrete* variables, `scale_fill_viridis_d` for continuous ## Many other themes ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-53-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: `theme_spongeBob()` from `tvthemes` package, many more online

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
